newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian premier quits, party factions battle.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian premier quits, party factions battle.

text.p: Bulgarian Prime Minister Zhan Videnov presented his resignation at a party congress on Saturday, intensifying a battle between hardliners and reformists for the future direction of the government.
Videnov pledged he would not seek re-election as premier or party leader but delegates said the congress could ask him to run again.
"If the declaration made by Zhan Videnov is not a tactical manoeuvre then I welcome it. I think it has been delayed too long," former party chairman Alexander Lilov told the congress.

U.S.-born Georgi Pirinski, who resigned as foreign minister last month saying the government lacked public support, had been tipped as a possible successor to Videnov but delegates said his star seemed to be waning.
The congress, which is expected to name a new cabinet, is likely to continue until late into Sunday night or early Monday.
Reformist delegates' speeches painted a bleak picture of an economy wrecked by seven years of delayed reform.
Acting foreign minister Irina Bokova said an increasingly isolationist Bulgaria no longer had the confidence of international financial or political institutions.
"Our foreign partners do not believe in our honest desire to integrate Bulgaria into European structures," she said.
Leading members of the Bulgarian Communist Party renamed themselves Socialists after the end of one-party rule in 1989.

The government's failure to meet reform targets including closing or restructuring loss-making state enterprises has led to the suspension of funding from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.
Attacks on Videnov's government, which is half way through its four-year term, became more vocal after the Socialist candidate's defeat in last month's presidential election.

A marathon 20-hour party plenum last month gave Videnov only narrow backing in a confidence vote and the premier is also under fire over his connections to a shady group of companies known as the Orion Group.

The deputy head of parliament's commission against corruption, Edvin Sugarev, wrote to the chief prosecutor on Thursday asking him to investigate Videnov's links to Orion and its bank, the Bulgarian Agricultural and Industrial Bank, which Sugarev said had caused significant losses to state and private financial institutions.

A quarter of Bulgaria's numerous and illiquid banks are in receivership. Loss of confidence in the banking system caused a run on the lev, which has fallen from 70 to the dollar at the beginning of the year to 485 now.
Orion was at the centre of a political row last year after Bulgaria exported large quantities of grain for high world prices, creating shortages at home.

Videnov has denied in parliament that there are any formal links between the companies, known as the Orion Group because they bear the names of stars in the Orion constellation. He says there are only "a friendly circle".

Influential former prime minister Andrei Lukanov, who was shot dead outside his home on October 2, was about to reveal high-level government corruption when he was killed, according to his party colleagues.

In the short term, governemnt upheaval may further delay economic reform. IMF technical experts left on Friday after helping the government to prepare the legal measures for setting up a currency board fixed exchange rate regime to halt the fall of the lev and to draft the 1997 budget framework.

Mission head Anne McGuirk said she hoped to be back in the New Year. "A lot depends on how long it takes to resolve the political situation and then we can come back and do the actual negotiation," she told reporters at the airport on Friday.
